coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage would mean: of the AWS services a customer runs internet-facing endpoints on, how many have at least one resource type Shield Advanced can protect. The page gives this only as a lossy roll-up, and the roll-up lies. Five services appear (CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, EC2, Elastic Load Balancing), but two of them are partial — Global Accelerator standard yes / custom routing no, and ELB ALB+CLB yes / NLB only via an Elastic IP / Gateway Load Balancer no — so a service-level Yes for either is false in specific, named cases. There is also no denominator: the page never enumerates the AWS services Shield Advanced does not reach, beyond the closed-world sentence implying all of them. So: service coverage is derivable as a five-name list with two entries flagged partial, and is NOT expressible as a ratio.

REGION coverage would mean: in which AWS Regions Shield Advanced can protect these resource types, and whether the answer differs by Region. The page gives NOTHING. Not one Region is named. There is no availability table, no per-Region qualifier on any bullet, and no statement about which of these resource types are global scope versus Regional (CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator are global in practice, but this page never says so, and inferring it is inventing content). Any Region figure sourced from this page would be fabricated, and the correct record is an explicit null with a note that Region availability must come from a different source.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage would mean: which AWS resource types Shield Advanced protects and which it does not. This is the page's native axis and the one thing it supplies in full — 8 supported and 3 explicitly excluded, 11 enumerated in total, with the protection method distinguishing 6 direct from 2 transitive-via-Elastic-IP (plus CloudFront staging distributions transitive via the primary distribution). The unusual strength here is the closed-world clause: "You can't use Shield Advanced to protect any other resource type" means the allow-list is complete, so every AWS resource type outside the 8 is a No, and the 3 named exclusions are illustrations rather than the full negative set. That still does not produce a percentage, because the universe of AWS resource types has no fixed denominator on this page. Record it as a complete allow-list with a closed-world flag and 3 confirmed named exclusions, never as a ratio.

features.collapse: The page names 11 things: eight it protects and three it does not. They are eight CloudFormation resource types. Application, Classic and Network Load Balancers are two types, not three, and a Gateway Load Balancer is the same type as the Application and Network ones — so that type reads partial, protected for some load balancers and not others. A custom routing accelerator is likewise the same type as the standard accelerator Shield does protect, so that reads partial too. NAT Gateway is the only exclusion with a type of its own, and reads not-covered.
features.featureName: Shield Advanced protections for each resource type ("List of resources that AWS Shield Advanced protects")
features.reasoning: The values are AWS resource types, not services: the page deliberately splits within a single service where the answers differ. Elastic Load Balancing yields three separate answers (ALB yes directly, CLB yes directly, NLB yes only via an Elastic IP) plus a fourth excluded one (Gateway Load Balancer). AWS Global Accelerator yields standard accelerators yes and custom routing accelerators no. Collapsing to a service axis would destroy exactly the information the page exists to convey. The axis is external because AWS resource types exist independently of Shield Advanced — Shield Advanced selects from that universe rather than publishing it, which is what makes a No meaningful here.
features.scope: Protection method: protected directly vs protected "through association with protected resources". Direct: CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, Global Accelerator standard accelerators, EC2 Elastic IP addresses, Application Load Balancers, Classic Load Balancers. Via association to a protected Elastic IP address: Amazon EC2 instances, Network Load Balancers. Via association to a protected primary distribution: CloudFront staging distributions. The page also names protection layers (network/transport layers 3 and 4, and application layer 7) but does not break them down per resource type, so layer is not a usable second dimension here.
features.statuses: 8 supported, 3 explicitly not supported. Supported (counted off the bullet list): 1 Amazon CloudFront distributions, 2 Amazon Route 53 hosted zones, 3 AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerators, 4 Amazon EC2 Elastic IP addresses, 5 Amazon EC2 instances, 6 Application Load Balancers, 7 Classic Load Balancers, 8 Network Load Balancers. Not supported, stated in prose Notes rather than a Yes/No column: 9 AWS Global Accelerator custom routing accelerators ("you can't protect"), 10 Gateway Load Balancers (same sentence), 11 NAT Gateways ("handle outbound traffic only, whereas Shield Advanced protects against inbound DDoS"). The exclusion list is introduced by a closed-world statement — "You can't use Shield Advanced to protect any other resource type" — so anything absent from the 8 is a No, and the 3 named ones are worked examples of that No, not the whole of it. CloudFront staging distributions under continuous deployment are a sub-case of CloudFront distributions, not a 9th type: they inherit protection from the protected primary distribution.

features.featureName: Shield Advanced IP version support ("Shield Advanced supports IPv4, and does not support IPv6")
features.reasoning: This is a genuine coverage claim of the shape "capability X reaches Y / does not reach Y" over an enumerable external set — the IP version universe is IPv4 and IPv6, and it exists independently of AWS. It is a separate capability from the resource-type list because the axis values are different and the statement applies across all resource types rather than to any one of them. It is small but it is not noise: an IPv6-only endpoint gets nothing from Shield Advanced, and that fact appears nowhere else on the page. A parser that only walks bullet lists and tables will miss it entirely, because it is a bare sentence in the opening paragraph.
features.statuses: 1 supported, 1 not supported. IPv4 supported, IPv6 not supported. Both stated in one sentence in the intro paragraph: "Shield Advanced supports IPv4, and does not support IPv6."
features.waived: Two members, so it cannot carry a denominator anyone can read. The page's statement that Shield Advanced supports IPv4 and not IPv6 belongs as a qualifier, not an axis. See the tiny-axis rule in stage6-validate.

pageTitle: List of resources that AWS Shield Advanced protects
shouldNotExtract: The "Introducing a new console experience for AWS WAF" banner and its Working with the console link — site chrome, present on every page in this guide. The quota paragraph: "up to 1,000 resources for each resource type per AWS account", the worked example of 1,000 EIPs plus 1,000 distributions plus 1,000 ALBs, and the Service Quotas console link — 1,000 is a limit, not a count of anything, and a parser that reads it as a coverage number produces nonsense. The Note that Shield Advanced "protects only resources that you have specified either in Shield Advanced or through an AWS Firewall Manager Shield Advanced policy. It doesn't automatically protect your resources." — that is an activation caveat about opt-in behaviour, not a claim about which things can be reached. The remediation pointer to AWS Network Firewall for outbound traffic — Network Firewall is a different service and must not be recorded as Shield Advanced coverage; only the NAT Gateway exclusion that precedes it is coverage. The layer 3/4 and layer 7 sentence as a standalone axis — it is scope-setting prose with no per-value breakdown. The entire "See also" section, including the AWS-appended boilerplate bullet about skills for AI coding assistants and the aws agent-toolkit search-skills command — pure appended boilerplate on every current AWS docs page. No Topics block, code examples, prerequisites, pricing, or troubleshooting exist on this page.
trap: Reading the axis as SERVICES instead of resource types. The bullets name five services — CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, EC2, ELB — and a careless parser emits five supported services and stops. That is wrong in both directions: it claims ELB is covered when Gateway Load Balancers are explicitly excluded, and claims Global Accelerator is covered when custom routing accelerators are explicitly excluded. The second trap is where the exclusions live: there is no Yes/No column, so every No sits in prose inside a **Note** block, and a bullet-harvesting parser returns 8 supported and 0 unsupported, losing the entire negative half of the page plus the closed-world sentence that makes the list authoritative. Third: flattening the nested ELB bullet, whose parent line is a heading rather than a value. Fourth: marking Amazon EC2 instances and Network Load Balancers as directly protectable when both require association to a protected Elastic IP address. Fifth: minting "CloudFront staging distribution" as a separate type from a conditional clause. Sixth: taking 1,000 from the quota paragraph as a count.
whatThePageStates: The page states which AWS resource types AWS Shield Advanced can protect against DDoS, and which it cannot. It gives a bulleted allow-list of protectable resource types, marks two of them as protected only through association with a protected Amazon EC2 Elastic IP address, and then closes the list with an explicit "You can't use Shield Advanced to protect any other resource type", naming Global Accelerator custom routing accelerators and Gateway Load Balancers as examples, plus a separate note excluding NAT Gateways because Shield Advanced protects inbound traffic only. It also states one protocol fact: Shield Advanced supports IPv4 and does not support IPv6. The rest of the page is a console banner, a per-account quota of 1,000 resources per resource type, and a See also block.
